item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ford (F.N) is recalling 102,159 F-Series trucks in the US over faulty equipment, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said on Tuesday. Here are details: The analog tachometer, which shows engine speed in revolutions per minute, and speedometer may get stuck or move erratically and provide inaccurate readings, NHTSA said The recall covers certain 2025-2026 F-250 SD, F-350 SD, F-450 SD, F-550 SD, F-600, and 2026 F-150 and F-750 SD trucks Dealers will replace the instrument cluster modules free of charge, the agency said

item.title: Wall Street gains as healthcare stocks rally, oil prices fall
item.description: Wall Street's main indexes climbed on Tuesday as healthcare stocks hit a record high and easing oil prices boosted investor sentiment, while markets continued to stabilize following last week's technology-led selloff.
item.dc:creator: Tharuniyaa Lakshmi, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: Wall Street's main indexes climbed on Tuesday as healthcare stocks hit a record high and easing oil prices boosted investor sentiment, while markets continued to stabilize following last week's technology-led selloff. Brent crude was trading 1.3% lower, reversing course after touching a near five-month high earlier in the day. Most S&P 500 constituents gained, with healthcare (.SPXHC) and financials (.SPSY) rising 1.8% and 1%, respectively. Energy led the losses, while an about 2% decline in Meta Platforms (META.O) pulled the communication services (.SPLRCL) sector down. The market extended Monday's rebound, when the S&P 500 (.SPX) and Nasdaq (.IXIC) climbed as investors bought the dip in technology stocks after last week's sharp selloff, fueled in part by concerns over CoreWeave's (CRWV.O) debt load and the cost of financing the AI buildout. AI-related shares were flat to higher on Tuesday, after showing weakness in premarket trading. CoreWeave was last up 1.6%, while chip gauge Philadelphia Semiconductor index (.SOX) rose 0.4%. "You're seeing some strength in some high-value stocks and the Dow, and so that's helping to sort of lift the overall index," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. "Concerns about what's going on as far as semiconductors, that's still there and AI-related names are down, but for the most part, the rest of the market is seeing a bit of a nice rebound." Elsewhere, shares of South Korean AI infrastructure company Elice Group (0158S0.KQ) [USN:L1N466008 TEXT:"tumbled nearly 30% in their market debut"], slipping below their IPO price after the company raised 201.1 billion won ($151.12 million) in its offering. At 10:31 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 617.62 points, or 1.22%, to 52,599.29. The S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 53.99 points, or 0.70%, to 7,744.72, while the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) added 154.58 points, or 0.59%, to 26,585.47. Investors are now watching this week's corporate earnings for clues on whether companies can maintain strong growth in the face of mounting macroeconomic risks. Quarterly results from SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Netflix (NFLX.O) are due after the market close on Tuesday, while heavyweights Meta Platforms (META.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) are scheduled to report on Wednesday. Steel Dynamics (STLD.O) fell 1% after the [USN:L4N4651KV TEXT:"steelmaker missed"] third-quarter profit estimates. General Motors (GM.N) shares dropped 5.3% after the automaker forecast its annual earnings below [USN:L6N4660PI TEXT:"analysts' expectations"]. 3M (MMM.N) gained 5.3% after the [USN:L4N4651MW TEXT:"company said"] it was expanding its data-center partnership with Amazon (AMZN.O) , and issued a warrant to an Amazon subsidiary to purchase 3M common stock worth over $521 million. The industrial conglomerate also raised its full-year profit forecast on Tuesday. Credit reporting firm Equifax (EFX.N) jumped 9.6% after it reported third-quarter profit above analysts' estimates. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.55-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by 3.45-to-1 on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 21 new 52-week highs and one new low, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 26 new highs and 183 new lows.

item.title: Aerospace and military contractors raise 2026 profit forecasts
item.description: Northrop Grumman and RTX raised their annual profit forecasts on Tuesday, helped by robust demand from military programs that pushed their backlogs to record levels.
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Singh, Aatreyee Dasgupta, Mike Stone
item.content:encoded: Northrop Grumman (NOC.N) and RTX (RTX.N) raised their annual profit forecasts on Tuesday, helped by robust demand from military programs that pushed their backlogs to record levels. Sustained demand for commercial aerospace services also fueled growth, both at [USN:L4N4660T1 TEXT:"RTX"] and rival engine maker [USN:L4N4660OA TEXT:"GE Aerospace"] (GE.N) , which lifted its full-year forecast for a second time this year. Northrop shares jumped by 7.2% in early trading and RTX gained 2.4% while GE Aerospace lost 4.9% on lower than expected implied fourth-quarter earnings. GEOPOLITICAL BACKDROP BRINGS SUSTAINED MILITARY SPENDING The results add to strong performances among US aerospace and defense contractors, supported by airline maintenance spending, growing demand for aircraft engines and parts and sustained military spending at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions around the globe. Sales at RTX's Raytheon climbed 14%, driven by higher volume in naval programs and land and air defense systems, including Patriot, Standard Missile and Tomahawk. "We continue to see robust global demand for all of our products and services," RTX finance chief Neil Mitchill told Reuters on Tuesday, adding that the company had "another record backlog" of $340 billion, up 36% from a year ago. [USN:L4N4660MP TEXT:"Northrop"], which makes the B-21 Raider bomber and parts for F-35 fighter jets, registered a similar 14% sales increase at its Aeronautics Systems unit, which benefited from increased B-21 sales and higher F-35 production. The company secured $16.4 billion in new contracts during the quarter, with its orders growing at 1.5 times its billings, driven by strong demand across programs including Sentinel, the F-35, Virginia-class submarines and certain classified programs. Northrop's backlog rose to a record $109.6 billion by September 30. Similarly, RTX chalked up $81 billion in new commercial and defense awards, pushing its backlog to a record $340 billion. Beyond the military sphere, RTX was helped by airline maintenance spending and growing demand for its Pratt & Whitney aircraft engines and parts even as surging fuel costs squeeze airline profits. GE Aerospace registered similarly firm demand, with revenue at its commercial engines and services business rising more than a fifth to $10.34 billion. It acknowledged, however, that prolonged high fuel prices could lead airlines to reduce flying, weakening demand for engine repairs, spare parts and spare engines. Northrop now expects full-year 2026 adjusted profit per share in the range of $29.35 to $29.75, up from a previous forecast of between $28.60 and $29.10. RTX now forecasts 2026 adjusted earnings per share of $7.65 to $7.75, up from its previous projection of $7.10 to $7.25. It also raised its sales forecast range to between $97 billion and $97.5 billion, from $95 billion to $96 billion. GE Aerospace now expects adjusted earnings of $8.00 to $8.10 per share in 2026, up from its previous forecast of $7.65 to $7.85 and above analyst expectations of $7.92, according to data compiled by LSEG.

item.title: Britain seeks to break Apple's grip on contactless payments
item.description: Britain's competition regulator said on Tuesday it was seeking to loosen Apple's grip on contactless payments by proposing that the company lower fees and remove technical barriers, helping rival services compete with Apple Pay.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sandle
item.content:encoded: Britain's competition regulator said on Tuesday it was seeking to loosen Apple's grip on contactless payments by proposing that the company lower fees and remove technical barriers, helping rival services compete with Apple Pay. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said its proposals would result in "substantially lower access fees" and easier access to Apple's contactless technology. The measures are less onerous than those imposed by the European Union in 2024, which included free access for third-party developers. Companies including PayPal, Klarna, Curve and BBVA have since launched alternative payment apps, the CMA said. 'HIGH FEES, STRICT TERMS' The EU commitments require Apple to give wallet developers access to the iPhone's NFC chip using host card emulation (HCE), allowing third-party apps to process contactless payments without going through Apple Pay or Apple Wallet. The CMA's proposals would give developers access to HCE in addition to Apple's existing secure element (SE) technology. The regulator can impose requirements on Apple after designating it and Google as having strategic market status in smartphones last year. Contactless payments account for 39% of all payments, compared with 3% a decade ago, the CMA said. More than 60% of adults use a digital wallet, with Apple Wallet the most popular in Britain. CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said the proposals would boost innovation, consumer choice and Britain's fintech sector. "We have heard that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions relating to Apple's contactless technology make it too difficult for challengers to innovate and compete," she said. The CMA is consulting on the proposals until November 17, before making a final decision. Digital bank Revolut welcomed the proposals, saying access to NFC technology through HCE was critical. "The CMA's direction creates a real opportunity for UK fintechs to compete on an equal footing with Big Tech," said Revolut's chief commercial officer, David Tirado. Apple said developers could already offer contactless payments through its NFC technology and secure element, which stores sensitive information such as card credentials and cryptographic keys. It said this enabled services including in-store payments, transit passes and event tickets while protecting users' data. "We do not believe the CMA should require Apple to adopt an approach with lower privacy and security protections," an Apple spokesperson said. "We will continue to engage constructively to reach an outcome that is in the best interest of our users."

item.title: Colombian Congress approves budget allocations, cuts funding to peace deal
item.description: Colombian lawmakers approved spending distributions for next year's 634.9 trillion pesos ($201.14 billion) budget early on Tuesday, trimming spending linked to a 10-year-old peace agreement and boosting debt service payments.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Colombian lawmakers approved spending distributions for next year's 634.9 trillion pesos ($201.14 billion) budget early on Tuesday, trimming spending linked to a 10-year-old peace agreement and boosting debt service payments. The budget, which projects a 2027 fiscal deficit of 9.4% of gross domestic product, is a significant increase from the 555.8 trillion peso budget for this year. The bill allocates 141 trillion pesos, about $45 billion for debt repayment next year, up from about $30 billion allocated in 2026. Neither congress nor the finance ministry had published a complete breakdown of the approved budget by morning on Tuesday and a congressional source told Reuters a final version could take days, as some modifications were approved by only one of the chambers. The bigger budget comes as Colombia, Latin America's fourth-largest economy, struggles to put its public accounts in order. Public debt is expected to rise this year and next, moving the country further from regaining the investment-grade rating it lost in 2021. The government of new right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella had promised to trim remaining spending for this year and said it plans to propose a 'Rescue Law' to Congress to cut 2027 spending and reduce the fiscal deficit to 7.2% of GDP. Lawmakers in the lower house approved the bill with 112 votes in favor and only one against it, while in the Senate it passed with 57 votes in favor and one against. Lawmakers had until Tuesday night to pass the budget before it would be possible for the government to put it through via decree. "Thank you all for giving us this vote of confidence. We are going to succeed in getting the country out of this very complex economic situation," Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said after the Senate passed the bill late on Monday night. SPENDING CUTS The budget cuts funds for the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) - the court created under a 2016 peace deal with the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) guerrillas to try rebel leaders and ex-soldiers for war crimes - by some 181 billion pesos, the finance ministry said in a statement, and reassigns that money to the defense ministry. The cut amounts to 23% of the court's budget, an even deeper reduction than had been previously expected. Several lawmakers said the budget for the Search Unit for Disappeared People (UBPD), created under the peace deal to look for at least 137,000 people who vanished during the ongoing armed conflict, had also been cut, but there were not yet final figures showing by how much. The two entities and advocates have said cuts will [USN:L6N45R12F TEXT:"limit investigations and trials"] into human rights violations, as well as exhumations and identifications of the disappeared. ($1 = 3,156.50 Colombian pesos)

item.title: Congreso de Colombia aprueba presupuesto de gastos para 2027 por 634,9 billones de pesos
item.description: El Congreso de Colombia aprobó el martes el presupuesto de gastos para 2027 por 634,9 billones de pesos (201.168 millones de dólares), que contempla una reasignación de recursos entre diferentes sectores, un recorte en rubros relacionados con el acuerdo de paz y un incremento de los recursos destinados al pago del servicio de la deuda.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El Congreso de Colombia aprobó el martes el presupuesto de gastos para 2027 por 634,9 billones de pesos (201.168 millones de dólares), que contempla una reasignación de recursos entre diferentes sectores, un recorte en rubros relacionados con el acuerdo de paz y un incremento de los recursos destinados al pago del servicio de la deuda. La cifra supera los 555,8 billones de pesos del presupuesto vigente para 2026. El presupuesto del próximo año prevé un déficit fiscal de 9,4% del Producto Interno Bruto (PIB). El Senado aprobó la ley de presupuesto el lunes en la noche con 57 votos a favor y uno en contra, mientras que la Cámara de Representantes lo hizo el martes en la madrugada con 112 votos a favor y uno en contra. "Gracias a todos ustedes por habernos dado este voto de confianza, vamos a lograr sacar al país de esta situación económica tan compleja y para eso el presupuesto, sin lugar a dudas, es un primer paso muy importante", dijo el ministro de Hacienda, Miguel Gómez, después de la aprobación en el Senado. El Gobierno planea presentar al Congreso la denominada "Ley de Rescate" para recortar el gasto público el próximo año, con lo que el déficit fiscal se ajustaría al 7,2% del PIB, según el Ministerio de Hacienda. El presupuesto de gastos de 2027 asigna 141 billones de pesos (44.672 millones de dólares) para el pago de la deuda, 93 billones de pesos (29.465,6 millones de dólares) para educación, 84,6 billones de pesos (26.803 millones de dólares) para salud y 74,9 billones de pesos (23.739,3 millones de dólares) para defensa. La reasignación de recursos realizada por el Gobierno del presidente Abelardo De La Espriella provocó un recorte en el presupuesto de funcionamiento de la Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (JEP) y la Unidad de Búsqueda de Personas dadas por Desaparecidas (UBPD), creadas en virtud del acuerdo de paz de 2016 firmado con la antigua guerrilla de las Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (FARC). El recorte a la JEP fue de alrededor de 181.000 millones de pesos, recursos que se trasladaron al Ministerio de Defensa, según el Ministerio de Hacienda. Varios legisladores señalaron que también se recortó el presupuesto de la UBPD, que busca localizar a por lo menos 137.000 personas desaparecidas durante el conflicto armado, aunque aún no se conocen las cifras definitivas sobre la magnitud de la disminución. La decisión limitaría las investigaciones y los juicios por violaciones de los derechos humanos, así como la búsqueda de las personas desaparecidas en el conflicto armado, que continúa y ha dejado más de 450.000 muertos. La cuarta economía de América Latina enfrenta grandes desafíos para poner en orden sus cuentas fiscales, lo que elevará su endeudamiento público este año y el próximo, y la alejará cada vez más de la posibilidad de recuperar el grado de inversión que perdió en 2021. Además, el país sudamericano busca un acuerdo con el Fondo Monetario Internacional para conseguir financiamiento más barato y enfrentar el complicado panorama económico. Hasta la mañana del martes, ni el Congreso ni el Ministerio de Hacienda habían publicado un desglose completo del presupuesto aprobado. Una fuente del Congreso aseguró a Reuters que la versión definitiva podría tardar días en estar lista, dado que algunas modificaciones fueron aprobadas únicamente por una de las cámaras. (1 dólar = 3.156,32 pesos)

item.title: Germany's Merz touts defence, AI and chip investment drive in pitch to investors
item.description: Germany is investing heavily in sectors including defence, semiconductors and AI to boost its long-term productivity and economic sovereignty, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday as he pitched Europe's largest economy to investors.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Germany is investing heavily in sectors including defence, semiconductors and AI to boost its long-term productivity and economic sovereignty, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday as he pitched Europe's largest economy to investors. "Our goal is to create the best possible parameters for you," Merz said at the event in Berlin, pledging to cut red tape, speed up approvals and upgrade infrastructure. Merz is seeking to attract investment by emerging industries as high costs, red tape and a [USN:SPN45A00B TEXT:"sluggish recovery"] weigh on Germany's traditional industrial base. Firms in attendance included lithium and renewable energy firm Vulcan Energy and defence company Helsing. The economy ministry said companies including Amazon (AMZN.O) and Nvidia (NVDA.O) [USN:L8N4660WK TEXT:"pledged "]more than €225 billion ($252 billion) as part of the summit. In a swipe at the far-left leader seeking to become mayor of Berlin, [USN:L8N45D1DV TEXT:"Elif Eralp,"] who has pledged to expropriate corporate landlords, Merz said property rights underpinned Germany's economic order and "are not to be tampered with". Germany is already seeing positive economic effects from its policies, said Merz, pointing to stronger growth, rising foreign [USN:L8N4650JJ TEXT:"direct investment"] and increased startup creation. He highlighted the Made for Germany initiative, under which German companies have pledged to invest over €800 billion ($898.40 billion) by 2028. Merz said deeper European economic integration would help companies tap the European Union's single market and pledged to introduce EU Inc., a harmonised European corporate framework, as soon as possible. Germany aims to quadruple its artificial intelligence computing capacity by 2030 as part of a broader push to strengthen technological competitiveness, he added. Merz said he was personally "engaged on the European level" to ensure AI regulation "is opening the door and not closing the door before it happens." ($1 = 0.8905 euros)

item.title: Plus de 150 morts lors d'une attaque à la frontière entre Soudan et Soudan du Sud - ministre
item.description: Cent cinquante-trois personnes ont été tuées par des frappes de drones sur un marché d'Abiyé, région riche en pétrole située à la frontière entre le Soudan du Sud et le Soudan et revendiquée par les deux pays, a déclaré mardi le ministre de l'Information par intérim de la région.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Cent cinquante-trois personnes ont été tuées par des frappes de drones sur un marché d'Abiyé, région riche en pétrole située à la frontière entre le Soudan du Sud et le Soudan et revendiquée par les deux pays, a déclaré mardi le ministre de l'Information par intérim de la région. Ce dernier avait dans un premier temps fait état de 73 morts et 19 blessés. Des responsables du Soudan du Sud ont accusé l'armée soudanaise d'être responsable de cette attaque. La région d'Abiyé, administrée de manière conjointe par le Soudan et le Soudan du Sud, est régulièrement le théâtre de flambées de violences. L'année dernière, six soldats bangladais de la force de maintien de la paix des Nations unies ont été tués et huit autres blessés lors d'une attaque de drones menée par des groupes armés séparatistes contre une base de l'Onu à Abiyé. Le ministère des Affaires étrangères du Soudan du Sud a dit dans un communiqué publié lundi soir que des drones avaient frappé un marché situé au nord de la ville d'Abiyé, sans toutefois préciser le nombre de victimes civiles causées par cette attaque. Le ministère a ajouté avoir convoqué l'ambassadeur soudanais afin de lui faire part de la "vive protestation et de la profonde inquiétude" du gouvernement "concernant cette attaque et ses implications pour la sécurité des civils et la stabilité de la région d'Abiyé". L'organisation humanitaire Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) a dit dans un communiqué qu'elle avait pris en charge plus de 20 blessés à l'hôpital voisin d'Ameth Bek.

item.title: As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors, regulators raise flags
item.description: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Brown
item.content:encoded: For Allison Vecchio, 42, GLP-1 drugs were "a reset button on life," but at a price — side effects like gastrointestinal distress, brittle nails, and feelings of weakness so intense that at times she could not leave her bed. But the Fort Pierce, Florida-based ER nurse said the symptoms eased when she began a cocktail of supplements that included fiber, collagen and electrolytes, a haul that costs $200 to $300 a month. "You really have to take the reins" to turn mere weight loss into improved health, she said. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO) Ozempic and Wegovy rank among the biggest medical breakthroughs in years, owing to their efficacy in treating obesity and type 2 diabetes, and reducing the risk of heart disease. Some 10 million Americans used them last year, a figure that could grow to 25 million by 2030, according to JPMorgan research. Their side effects, though, have caused many to turn to loosely regulated dietary supplements. US supplement sales have surged in recent years, surpassing $74 billion in 2025, according to the Nutrition Business Journal. While users swear by them, their growing popularity — fueled in part by social media — has doctors raising red flags and regulators considering new rules around how these products come to market. Vitamins and supplements don't need preapproval by the US Food and Drug Administration, making their scientific credibility hard to gauge. With social media personalities playing a growing role in their promotion, some medical researchers have called for more regulation of online supplement marketing. Rob Fried, CEO of Niagen Bioscience (NAGE.O) , which had $129 million in sales last year, cautioned that companies "can hire an influencer, or even hundreds of influencers on TikTok ... to make whatever claims will sell." SALES OF SUPPLEMENTS SOAR Vecchio has 25,000 TikTok followers and is on retainer with three brands. She is also a member of TikTok Shop's HealthPro creator program, which is reserved for licensed health professionals. Pittsburg, Kansas, resident Terri Hart, 52 — a TikToker with more than 12,000 followers — mostly works on commission, perusing products the brands make available to influencers, and promoting the ones she feels helped her the most. Hart takes magnesium, electrolytes, B12 and other supplements, which she says have helped offset what she called "horrible" nausea, fatigue and constipation after beginning GLP-1s in 2023. They run about $110 a month, costs insurance doesn't cover. TikTok income eases the burden, Hart says. She says she makes clear she isn't a medical professional, and urges followers to talk to doctors before taking her advice. "I establish my authority through my lived experience," Hart said. TikTok Shop generated more than $1 billion in dietary supplement sales in 2025, or 5.4% of all e-commerce supplement sales, according to the Nutrition Business Journal, while overall US vitamin and supplement sales grew 5% in 2024 and 7% last year. The drugs are "bringing in new consumers and expanding existing supplement routines," said Erika Craft, a data analyst at Nutrition Business Journal. But absent FDA preapproval, people don't know exactly what is in many supplements, said Jonathan Bonnet, a clinical associate professor at Stanford and chief medical officer at the Ardmore Institute of Health in Ardmore, Oklahoma. "If you can't know what you're taking, it's hard to know what risks you're undergoing," he said. RETAILERS OFFER MORE SUPPLEMENTS Nearly half of GLP-1 users started taking new vitamins and supplements after beginning the drugs, according to a Nutrition Business Journal survey, with probiotics, protein and fiber particularly popular. A consumer survey by Boston Consulting Group this year said GLP-1 users spend roughly 20% more on protein, fiber and collagen, a protein that helps maintain skin structure, than before starting the drugs. Companies are capitalizing. Target (TGT.N) is widening its supplement offerings, while private equity-owned The Vitamin Shoppe has seen double-digit sales growth this year in fiber and creatine, which are both popular with GLP-1 users, said Jack Gayton, senior vice president of merchandising at The Vitamin Shoppe. Mergers and acquisitions in the space are getting bigger, though with fewer transactions. In 2024, there were 115 deals globally worth $7.3 billion, according to financial data firm PitchBook. In 2025, there were 95 deals worth $16.9 billion. Through October 6 of this year, there have been 68 deals worth $14.6 billion. Procter & Gamble (PG.N) is [USN:L4N4411L4 TEXT:"set to acquire"] supplement maker Thorne, while Japan's Kirin Holdings announced in August it will buy Canada's Jamieson Wellness (JWEL.TO) , whose US-based brand youtheory released a product aimed at GLP-1 users in early 2025. Jamieson spokesperson Ruth Winker said the company sees GLP-1s as a tailwind for growth beyond combating side effects. "As people get healthier, they tend to take more vitamins and supplements," Winker said. REGULATIONS IN THE OFFING US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has proposed tighter regulations. The FDA this year has stepped up efforts to strengthen oversight of new dietary ingredients, issuing new guidance on what submissions for review should include. Many supplement makers avoid this review process by using a pathway that allows food companies to declare ingredients “generally recognized as safe" without notifying the FDA. But a proposed rule would eliminate that option as part of Kennedy's broader effort to regulate food ingredients. The proposal has divided the industry. Some support more regulation, lamenting unscrupulous actors who spike supplements with drugs or add only tiny amounts of touted beneficial ingredients. “At a minimum, a review process should happen prior to launch," says Jacqueline Maslan, CEO of Body of Work, a vitamin startup aimed at women under 40. But supplement trade group the Council for Responsible Nutrition says the rule would cause months of backlogs as the FDA reviews thousands of ingredients. Thorne CEO Colin Watts said it's “improbable” the FDA could have the manpower to review new ingredients “at the speed needed to keep up with innovation." In a statement to Reuters, an HHS spokesperson said the FDA is mulling opportunities "to modernize its regulatory approach to keep pace with an evolving marketplace," adding the agency wants to ensure product safety "while supporting consumer choice."

item.title: UEFA demands answers from FIFA over Infantino presidency
item.description: UEFA has sent a letter to FIFA seeking answers by November 2 about Gianni Infantino's presidency, including questions over the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and the FIFA Peace Prize.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: UEFA has sent a letter to FIFA seeking answers by November 2 about Gianni Infantino's presidency, including questions over the [USN:L1N43X04P TEXT:"FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE)"] project and the [USN:L1N3XB0PC TEXT:"FIFA Peace Prize"]. European soccer's governing body UEFA has led calls for Infantino to resign since he proposed the now-abandoned FFE project, which involved creating a company to run the commercial interests of FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and selling a minority stake to private investors. The 56-year-old, who is up for reelection next year, apologised to the [USN:L8N4611Y3 TEXT:"FIFA Council"] last week and told attendees to submit any questions they had about his governance in writing so he could answer them at the next meeting on December 16. However, UEFA General Secretary Theodore Theodoridis wrote to his FIFA counterpart Mattias Grafstrom on Monday seeking a swift response to 42 questions covering 12 topics. "These questions require answers now," Theodoridis wrote. "They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the FIFA Council - nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them... "We expect FIFA to provide the transparency required by its own governing body and to respond fully within the above deadline." Reuters has seen a copy of the letter. "The FIFA Governance Regulations state that Council meetings and their associated documentation are confidential," a spokesperson for world soccer's governing body FIFA said on Tuesday. "While FIFA intends to reply to questions submitted by its Council members it has no intention of breaching confidentiality by commenting on internal communication and/or documentation to media. "FIFA considers respect for these Regulations to be a function of respect for the Council itself and for its individual members. FIFA will always maintain this respect and will not be drawn into any exchange with any third parties that undermines this." UEFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Infantino will stand for reelection in March 2027, with a November 18 deadline looming for potential candidates to submit their nominations.

item.title: Sudanese drone attack killed over 150 people in Abyei market, official says
item.description: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing over 150 people, one of the deadliest attacks in a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Sudanese officials said Sudan's military had carried out drone strikes that hit a market in the disputed Abyei region, killing over 150 people, one of the deadliest attacks in a war that has spilled across Sudan's borders. The strike showed the lethality of airstrikes in [USN:L6N40Y0KB TEXT:"Sudan's war"], which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), triggering a major humanitarian crisis and drawing in local militias and foreign powers. According to local authorities, the attack that hit the market in Abyei took place around midday on Monday. Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information in Abyei, told Reuters on Tuesday that the death toll had jumped to 153 from 73. He said Sudan's army was responsible for the attack, without providing evidence. A spokesperson for Sudan's armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Three diplomatic sources, an aid worker and an expert on the conflict told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market. The diplomatic sources said the depot had been used in the past by the RSF to supply its forces. A spokesperson for the RSF did not immediately respond to requests for comment. South Sudan declared independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have staked a claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. It borders Sudan's Kordofan region, which has become a major centre of fighting in Sudan's war. Officials in Sudan's military-led government told Reuters the RSF is active in parts of Abyei. Ngor denied the presence of the RSF in Abyei. Reuters could not immediately verify the claims. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) warned in May that the presence of the RSF in Abyei had increased insecurity there, adding that delays in determining the disputed region's final status had put civilians and UNISFA personnel at risk. STRUGGLE TO RETRIEVE BODIES Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes. "It has reached 153 — those we can confirm killed and the number will even rise (further)," he said. "The fire is still burning. So the recovery process of the dead ones is still continuing. The situation is terrible." Some 8,000 people had been displaced by Monday's bombing, Ngor added. South Sudan's foreign ministry said in a statement late on Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties. The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador in protest. Sudanese armed forces and the RSF have recently escalated [USN:L6N44V0K3 TEXT:"drone strikes"], with a series of attacks targeting RSF-held Nyala and army-held Khartoum airport this week. Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers said dozens of people were killed in attacks on October 17 and 18 in al-Muglad in West Kordofan state, attributing them to the Sudanese army. Chadian authorities have accused Sudan’s military of carrying out drone strikes on its territory, which UN experts say is regularly used by RSF supply lines. Sudan's foreign ministry said in late August that its armed forces were acting to protect the country's security. On October 10, [USN:L1N45X06E TEXT:"an airstrike"] close to Sudan's border with Egypt killed more than 70 artisanal miners, according to a local rights group. PATIENTS TREATED FOR BURNS Abyei experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias. The attack is the deadliest in years to hit the area, where medical supplies and healthcare are scarce. South Sudan's government says it has not taken sides in its neighbour's war. However, diplomats and experts say Abyei has established itself as crucial, serving as a transit point for RSF logistics, particularly fuel. Medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement posted late on Monday that it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital. "We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at Ameth Bek Hospital. Photographs shared on MSF's official social media account showed bandaged patients lying on the floor as they received care for their injuries.

item.title: France to deploy troops, admits to failures over weekend unrest
item.description: France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend's violence.
item.dc:creator: Elizabeth Pineau, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"last weekend's violence"]. "The deployment next Saturday will be massive," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17. In a sometimes rowdy debate, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centres had been left vulnerable. TARGETED CURFEWS HELP RESTORE CALM Framing the crisis as a choice "between violence and the Republic", Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating [USN:L1N4650EF TEXT:"public anger"] over high living costs and declining public services. The unrest shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls. Protests in other European countries, including [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"Italy"] and [USN:L6N464038 TEXT:"Albania"], have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes. A night of relative calm in France followed [USN:L6N4650BY TEXT:"targeted curfews"] imposed in several areas affected by the turmoil, which the government said had helped reassert control. In central Paris, police emptied and guarded the Place de la Republique overnight, with a helicopter overhead. In Lille, in the north, where the curfew only applied to minors, officers patrolled the city centre, checking bypassers' identities. Marseille mayor Benoit Payan said there would be curfews for minors around the commercial areas hardest hit by the weekend's riots, starting Tuesday night. Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state's response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had decided against cancelling planned police leave. Nunez apologised for the failings. "I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility," he said. SUSPECT ARRESTED FOR LIMOGES TOWN HALL DESTRUCTION Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence. Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group. Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, told Reuters some apps had become "a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters". Underscoring the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years. France's main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron's government over what it says is a deteriorating and underfunded education system. "We carry on," it said on social media. Separately, groups identifying themselves as "Gilets Jaunes" (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs. The yellow vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in 2018 during Macron's first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now. ITALY FACES NEW FORM OF UNREST, MINISTER SAYS Northern Italian cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend. Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government, which was expected to introduce new security measures at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of "hybrid warfare" conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other online networks. "The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras," Crosetto wrote on X. "The West has yet to realise this or take any meaningful action in response." In Milan's central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi's store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons. In Albania, protesters were expected to take to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

item.title: Rubio to encourage India's Reliance to produce, refine more Venezuelan oil
item.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio plans to encourage India's Reliance Industries to refine more Venezuelan crude at its local refineries and potentially begin producing oil in the South American country, he told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio plans to encourage India's Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) to refine more Venezuelan crude at its local refineries and potentially begin producing oil in the South American country, he told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday. Rubio landed in India's sweltering financial capital days after President Donald Trump waived potential sanctions on the world's top buyers of Russian oil, a list that includes India. The move is likely to help pave the way for a trade deal between New Delhi and Washington, but has been panned by US lawmakers, who complain that the Trump administration has been far too soft on Moscow. During the two-day visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar in the western part of the country, Rubio is slated to meet government and business leaders, including Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar and billionaire Mukesh Ambani, chairman of Reliance Industries, which operates the world's largest refining complex. "We will talk about (refining more Venezuelan crude) tomorrow with Reliance...They have done so in the past, and I think as more and more of Venezuelan oil comes online, that is something they can do," Rubio told reporters. Reliance's two massive refineries at the Jamnagar complex, with a combined capacity of about 1.4 million barrels per day of crude oil, are able to process the ultra-heavy crudes coming out of Venezuela, some of which have a sludge-like consistency. As Venezuela's oil production has increased following the Trump administration's capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January, Reliance has emerged as a significant importer of the nation's crude. Asked whether he would discuss the possibility of Reliance itself producing oil with Venezuela, Rubio said the matter had been discussed in the past, and that the matter would come up again. While Reliance is a major refiner of Venezuelan crude, it is not active inside the South American country. "We are going to go see what the holdup is and what opportunities exist...this is a company that has had a presence in Venezuela in the past, and whose refining capabilities are substantial," he said. NEW DELHI, WASHINGTON CLOSE IN ON TRADE DEAL Rubio's visit comes as Trump removed one potential stumbling block to a trade deal between the countries last Friday when he waived potential tariffs that would have punished New Delhi for its extensive purchases of Russian crude oil. Legislation signed by Trump in September authorizes the administration to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil, which would include India, which stands at number two on that list after China. Trump's decision to waive all substantive provisions of that bill has upset both Democrats and Republicans who have pushed him to up economic pressure on Moscow for its war with Ukraine. Rubio has said the effort to finalize a trade deal was a factor in the decision to waive those tariffs, and a comprehensive trade deal is almost complete, raising the possibility that it could be signed during his visit. He said the Trump administration was entering a 60-day review period, during which it would consider which new tariffs, if any, to impose. While the Trump administration has in the past pressed India to cut Russian oil imports, the US signed a deal with Russia last week to import diesel in a bid to cut domestic fuel prices before the midterm elections, making it unclear to what extent that remains a foreign policy priority. "Every country has a complex set of factors that they have to take into account," Rubio told reporters on Monday when asked about India's Russian oil purchases. India imports more than 85% of its crude oil requirements to help power its fast-growing economy. Rubio's India visit follows a trip to the Uzbekistan city of Samarkand, where he met Central Asian political and business leaders.

item.title: Gold steady as investors await fed rate signals
item.description: Gold prices were largely steady in a volatile session on Tuesday as investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve meeting for further direction on US interest rates.
item.dc:creator: Anushree Mukherjee
item.content:encoded: Gold prices were largely steady in a volatile session on Tuesday as investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve meeting for further direction on US interest rates. Spot gold was unchanged at $4,138.54 per ounce by 11:19 am EDT (1519 GMT). US gold futures for December delivery dropped 0.1% to $4,157.90 per ounce. "Inflation and the Fed's interest rates are the big stories that gold's fighting at the moment. US Treasuries do appear more favorable than gold as a safety asset for the moment," said Bob Haberkorn, senior market strategist at StoneX. "$4,000 is a big level for (gold) to keep an eye on and see if it can hold. A lot of that, at the moment, is going to be dependent on what the Fed says," Haberkorn said. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter point in September, its first hike this year. While recent comments from [USN:L6N462084 TEXT:"Fed"] officials signaling little [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"urgency"] for further policy tightening have tempered expectations of a rate hike at the central bank's October 27-28 policy meeting, traders see a 92% chance of a hike in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool . FEDWATCH Gold is still down around 26.4% from its record high of $5,594.82 in January and roughly 22% from levels at the start of the Iran war , when concerns over energy inflation reinforced bets on interest rate hikes. Gold is traditionally seen as an inflation hedge, but it loses its appeal as a non-yielding asset in a high-interest-rate environment. Investors are also watching next week's US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, for clues on whether inflation pressures remain persistent and how that could shape the rate outlook. In Japan, central bank Governor Kazuo Ueda [USN:L1N465004 TEXT:"said"] underlying inflation was "quite close" to the 2% target, signaling scope for further rate hikes. Among other metals, spot silver rose 1.5% to $57.92 per ounce, platinum gained 0.7% to $1,651.36 per ounce and palladium dropped 0.2% to $1,117.75 per ounce.

item.title: Dollar dips on AI worries, euro edges up despite French unrest
item.description: The US dollar slipped on Tuesday as doubts over the AI trade resurfaced, while the euro edged up despite traders' lingering worries about unrest in France.
item.dc:creator: Karen Brettell
item.content:encoded: The US dollar slipped on Tuesday as doubts over the AI trade resurfaced, while the euro edged up despite traders' lingering worries about unrest in France. Shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group (0158S0.KQ) plunged 32% in their Seoul [USN:L1N46600F TEXT:"market debut"], a sign that negative sentiment toward the AI sector in global markets is not easing. Strong capital inflows into US stocks have supported the dollar. Higher interest rates, driven partly by growth and inflation expectations tied to the sector, have also helped. "The dollar has been supported by big inflows into the equity market," said Dominic Bunning, head of G10 FX strategy at Nomura. Now, he said, "there is a lot more skepticism about the degree to which a lot of these companies will be profitable enough to justify the amount of issuance that having to be made at the moment … and whether this whole ecosystem can be profitable enough in the context of higher rates over a period of time." The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, fell 0.27% to 101.69, with the euro up 0.2% at $1.1232. Traders remained wary of the euro despite Tuesday's modest gains as France faces widespread protests and a worsening fiscal picture. The government said overnight curfews in violence-hit areas of France's biggest cities had brought [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"some respite"] from the country's worst unrest in years. More protests are planned for the weekend. "The worries in France are not going away anytime soon," said Tommy von Brömsen, FX strategist at Handelsbanken. "The bearish view on France will stay for a while longer, and there's much more euro weakness to be priced in." Britain's pound strengthened 0.66% to $1.339 after labour market data showed a resilient [USN:L8N46608R TEXT:"jobs market"], the latest batch of data from the UK that surprised to the upside. "The risk is that a resilient labour market gives the Bank of England both the room and the reason to raise interest rates again," said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. "Sterling could benefit from rising rate expectations." Markets are almost fully pricing in a 25-basis-point rate hike by the Bank of England at its next meeting on November 5, according to LSEG data. STRONG JAPANESE BOND AUCTION The yen jumped after an auction of longer-dated Japanese government bonds (JGBs) drew [USN:L1N46604J TEXT:"record demand"]. "The record 20-year auction is a strong signal that sidelined cash is finally coming back," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed-income strategist at State Street Investment Management in Tokyo. "JGBs are also starting to look like a relative haven from Europe's political and fiscal volatility, particularly around France.” The Japanese yen gained 0.29% against the greenback to 158.04 per dollar. Elsewhere, the Canadian dollar rose 0.42% to 1.405 per US dollar, its strongest level in almost a month, after Alberta residents voted by a [USN:L6N4651AT TEXT:"large majority"] to remain part of Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation.

item.title: Brent slips in choppy session as investors weigh attacks on ships, Saudi energy
item.description: Oil prices slipped from a five-month high during a choppy session on Tuesday as traders priced in Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
item.dc:creator: Georgina Mccartney
item.content:encoded: Oil prices slipped from a five-month high during a choppy session on Tuesday as traders priced in Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they launched [USN:S8N44M08Y TEXT:"several attacks"] on Saudi energy, airport and military targets, such as an Aramco (2222.SE) site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and Abha airport. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Houthi claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. Brent crude futures fell 67 cents or 0.61% to $108.88 at 10:09 a.m. EDT. Earlier in the session the front-month contract reached $111.99, a five-month high. The November contract for US West Texas Intermediate crude, which expires on Tuesday, was up 88 cents or 0.85% at $104.54, down from the session high of 110.48, the highest since April for a nearby contract. The more active December contract was down 45 cents or 0.46% at $98.09 a barrel. "Oil prices remain well-supported ... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over two weeks, which keeps the risk premium intact, shiptracker Kpler said in a note on Monday. Also on Monday, a Houthi [USN:L1N46509O TEXT:"attack"] on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200. The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel. DIESEL SUPPLY CRUNCH Russian diesel cargoes are returning to their traditional destinations after the [USN:L6N4660Q8 TEXT:"US suspended sanctions"] and secured the lifting of an export ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, according to shipping data from Kpler and LSEG. The US is [USN:L1N4660KS TEXT:"working with domestic refiners"] to squeeze more crude through the refining complex, US Energy Department Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit said on Tuesday at the Drake Forum in Titusville, Pennsylvania. In the US, analysts expected crude oil stockpiles to have fallen last week along with product inventories, a preliminary Reuters [USN:L4N4651EI TEXT:"poll"] showed on Monday.

item.title: South Korean firm's debut plunge adds to investor concerns about AI spending
item.description: A 32% drop in shares of South Korea's Elice Group on Tuesday renewed investor concerns about the sustainability and the payoff cycle for the vast amount of capital pouring into the AI buildout amid growing scrutiny of company valuations.
item.dc:creator: Heejin Kim, Yantoultra Ngui
item.content:encoded: A 32% drop in shares of South Korea's Elice Group (0158S0.KQ) on Tuesday renewed investor concerns about the sustainability and the payoff cycle for the vast amount of capital pouring into the AI buildout amid growing scrutiny of company valuations. The plunge in shares of the provider of AI cloud services as well as AI-based education and business software made it the worst debut ever in South Korea for a company that raised more than $100 million in an IPO, according to Dealogic data. Elice raised 201.1 billion won ($150 million) in its IPO, and said that it planned to spend most of the proceeds on launching portable modular data centres and related infrastructure. The stock's poor first day of trading contributed to [USN:L6N4660RT TEXT:"renewed weakness"] in AI-linked stocks on Wall Street on Tuesday, with shares in neocloud firms including CoreWeave (CRWV.O) and Nebius Group (NBIS.O) both falling more than 5%. Elice's slide had earlier weighed on the broader South Korean market, a poster child for global AI trade and investor sentiment, with the benchmark KOSPI (.KS11) falling 3.73% to its lowest closing level since April 7. After dominating market gains, AI companies are now facing more sceptical investors as concerns over spending, competition and profitability eclipse optimism about AI's long-term potential. Elevated inflation has also pushed interest rates higher, meaning the AI sector's debt will become more expensive to repay. S&P Global estimates the world's biggest tech firms are likely to have more [USN:L8N4651G6 TEXT:"AI-linked liabilities"] than currently known. Elice's IPO was priced on October 6, before the recent selloff in AI-related stocks. "The conclusion is simple: the timing is bad. The latest chip selloff has bruised investors' appetite, and the poor debut is certainly a warning for upcoming AI listings," said Swissquote analyst Ipek Ozkardeskaya. "The good news is that AI headlines could change from one minute to the next. One great development and the rally could be back," she said, adding the sector's upside potential continues to compete with the downside risks from high valuations. INCREASING SCRUTINY OF AI INFRA DEALS Elice's shares closed at 60,500 won compared with its IPO pricing of 90,500 won, leaving it valued at roughly 674 billion won ($508 million). The IPO drew institutional orders worth 388.84 times the shares available in the offering. Its poor debut came after other AI companies dropped or suspended deals in recent days, as investors reassess whether the firms racing to build the infrastructure underpinning AI can generate returns that justify [USN:L4N45Z0RI TEXT:"soaring spending"]. The IPO of Australia's [USN:L1N45U12T TEXT:"Firmus"], which is backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , was shelved, while Blackstone-backed (BX.N) [USN:L4N45Z0H4 TEXT:"AirTrunk"] postponed a Singapore listing, and [USN:L6N45H0SG TEXT:"SB Energy"], a unit of SoftBank (9984.T) , delayed its US share sale. Investors are increasingly scrutinising AI infrastructure and data centre deals, said Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based Shenton Research, and were now focused on those firms' customer contracts and committed revenue figures. "Everyone is not sure how much demand for AI there will be and it is hard to estimate current demand," said Kim Hak-joon, an analyst at Seoul-based Kiwoom Securities. Elice's revenue for the first half of the year tripled to 34 billion won and it swung to an operating profit of 10 billion won compared with a 3.5 billion won loss for the same period a year earlier. The company's largest shareholder is chief executive and co-founder Kim Jae Won, who holds 34.6%, ahead of Silicon Valley investor Altos with 24.45% and the Korea Development Bank, which owns 6.45%, according to company filings. ($1 = 1,327.2800 won)

item.title: Hegseth discusses Iran with Netanyahu in unannounced visit to Israel, officials say
item.description: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran . Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the prime minister, later confirmed to Reuters that Netanyahu had met with Hegseth at the Uvda air force base in Israel's southern Negev desert region. Netanyahu and Hegseth discussed "the threats in the region" and the US-Israel partnership in dealing both offensively and defensively with those threats, he said in a brief phone call. Hegseth also thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump's support for the prime minister. "There's a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion," Spielman said. On Sunday, Trump [USN:L1N46403J TEXT:"endorsed"] Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel, the country's first ballot since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel. The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Hegseth's visit. Hegseth earlier posted on X that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia. He did not specify where he had met with the forces. Hegseth's visit comes as tensions flare between the US and Iran over the [USN:S8N43Z00H TEXT:"Strait of Hormuz"] and as Yemen's Iran-allied [USN:S8N43T03Z TEXT:"Houthis intensify their attacks"] on Saudi Arabia. US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he's [USN:L1N4600GP TEXT:"not seeking to attack Iran"] before the October 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will [USN:FWN45U1SW TEXT:"not attack Iran"] before US midterm elections in November. Israel has hosted additional US forces, including military aircraft, since at least February as part of the war with Iran.

item.title: France in turmoil: What might follow a weekend of riots?
item.description: France is counting the cost of some of its worst unrest in years at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services. Here is the latest:
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: France is counting the cost of some of its [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"worst unrest in years"] at the weekend over the cost of living and under-funded public services. Here is the latest: HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT STOP MORE VIOLENCE AND HELP VICTIMS? Authorities say 2,500 people are in custody awaiting questioning while 149 are detained awaiting trial. [USN:L8N4650PE TEXT:"Partial curfews"] have been imposed in parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Lille, Lyon, Nice and Marseille to keep the streets quiet in areas worst-hit by rioting. The government, which had 60,000 officers mobilised at the weekend, plans to increase police numbers on the ground. For businesses and victims of violence, the government is implementing state-financed furlough measures to avoid layoffs, and providing funds to help companies meet cashflow needs. Insurers have promised speedy payouts to cover some of the damage, which hit more than 3,000 shops. HOW WILL THE GOVERNMENT ADDRESS UNDERLYING COMPLAINTS? France's extremely strained public finances mean the government has precious little room for broader measures to address protesters' anger over the rising cost of living. It has already hiked emergency spending this year to help certain sectors like farmers, fishermen and haulers cope with high fuel costs caused by the Iran war . The protests [USN:L1N45S0C7 TEXT:"began last month at high schools"] in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement. The government has so far not committed to substantial extra funding for schools but [USN:L6N45V0FM TEXT:"has pledged"] to send some 3,000 teachers, who are qualified but not yet working, to fill staffing gaps. HAVE PROTESTS PEAKED? Cities [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"were quieter"] at the start of the week. But some protesters have called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday. Unions have called for strikes on November 5 to protest budget cuts and support hiking wages. Schools are on a break for two weeks, but some student organisations are calling for more demonstrations. HOW WILL FRANCE'S DIRE ECONOMIC SITUATION BE AFFECTED? The unrest is a blow to business confidence, which was already fragile due to a fiscal crisis and high energy prices. The minority government is struggling to pass spending cuts in a divided parliament as part of its 2027 budget and is at risk of being toppled by opposition parties if a compromise cannot be found with at least some of them. The government wants to cut its budget deficit to 5.0% of economic output next year from 5.4% this year – one of the biggest in the euro zone. French bond yields [USN:L6N4660NP TEXT:"climbed further"] on Tuesday after their biggest daily rise in nearly a month in the previous session, with investors remaining cautious. The yield on France's 10-year benchmark bond reached 4.96% at one point on Tuesday. WILL THE UNREST SPREAD TO OTHER COUNTRIES? If France cannot contain the unrest, there is a risk that it could [USN:L8N4611KF TEXT:"spill across its borders"] with deep public anger around Europe over cost-of-living issues. In neighbouring Italy, [USN:L8N46407Z TEXT:"clashes erupted"] between police and protesters on Sunday. Albania has also seen a series of student demonstrations in recent days over corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, while Spain and Portugal have faced protests over housing. HOW WILL THE UNREST AFFECT THE 2027 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION? Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power. The unrest is likely to boost far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in polls and has long talked tough on law and order. "Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp, [USN:L6N4650JF TEXT:"told Reuters"]. "It's not just a clear path ahead of her, it's a six-lane highway." Hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has come under pressure for backing protesters' demands, criticising the government's handling and not clearly condemning the violence. Meanwhile, Macron, who headed off to the Middle East on Monday, has emerged from the crisis further weakened. His former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, now a centre-right presidential candidate, said on X he wanted "decisions and initiatives" from the lame-duck leader to "restore order". ARE PARIS AND OTHER CITIES SAFE TO VISIT? There have been no reports of any injuries to foreigners caught up in the unrest. However, several European governments [USN:L8N4650JR TEXT:"advised citizens"] travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution.

item.title: France's unrest lays bare 'slow agony' of Macron's twilight months
item.description: The civil unrest has exposed the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger.
item.dc:creator: Michel Rose
item.content:encoded: France’s worst bout of civil unrest in years has plunged President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office deeper into [USN:FWN4630KA TEXT:"turmoil"], exposing the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger with little money to spend, scant political capital and an increasingly fragile grip on public order. The [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"rioting"] that swept across France on Saturday, leaving a trail of looted shops, torched buildings and defaced public institutions, presents Macron with perhaps the most explosive challenge of his twilight presidency: a country demanding more from a state that can no longer afford to give much. Macron came to power almost a decade ago promising to upend France’s sclerotic political class, turbocharge economic reforms and restore authority through a more assertive presidency. Instead, with just six months left in office, he finds himself effectively a lame-duck head of state presiding over a country mired in political paralysis, facing acute [USN:L6N46502R TEXT:"financial pressures"] and grappling with unrest that has exposed the limits of state authority. Unlike during the Yellow Vest uprising of 2018-2019, when Macron sought to defuse public anger with billions of euros in concessions, France’s strained public finances and fractured parliament leave him with precious few levers to pull. Even former allies are now openly scathing, tracing the country's current impasse to Macron's decision to call a [USN:L8N3J00J1 TEXT:"snap parliamentary election"] in 2024 that weakened his authority. “The end of this term is a slow agony,” said Loïc Kervran, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp, on X. “The president paralysed the country with his absurd decision to dissolve parliament in 2024. Arguably the worst decision in the history of the Fifth Republic." LE PEN'S 'HIGHWAY' TO THE PRESIDENCY The turmoil may benefit far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race and stands to gain from both the anger over declining living standards and the fears over law and order unleashed by the weekend’s violence. "Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign," Jean-Baptiste Moreau, another former Macron lawmaker, told Reuters. "It's not just a clear path ahead of her — it's a six-lane highway." Le Pen delivered her own message to the nation in a video statement on Sunday, portraying Macron's administration as a crumbling power and casting herself as the figure capable of restoring order. When Macron later addressed the country, he offered little concrete action, stopping short of declaring a state of emergency. As he spoke, looting was continuing for a second consecutive night, including in affluent Paris districts, prompting his prime minister Sébastien Lecornu to announce local curfews on Monday. Opponents and one-time allies alike were underwhelmed. His former prime minister, Edouard Philippe, now preparing his own presidential run, was unsparing in his criticism. "Mr President, I listened to you last night," he wrote on X. "I would have preferred, like millions of French people, decisions and initiatives to restore order." "Our country needs to be commanded," he added. But even Philippe is struggling to shake off his past association with Macron, and most recent polls show far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon edging ahead of him in the race to qualify for the second-round runoff vote. That outcome would all but guarantee a Le Pen victory, according to opinion polls. CALLS FOR EARLY RESIGNATION AMID MULTIPLE CRISES Macron's office on Monday announced that he had refused his interior minister's resignation and ordered a review into apparent failures in intelligence gathering and police preparedness — deepening the impression of a government struggling to regain control. [USN:L1N465097 TEXT:"Investors also took fright"]. Market analysts say the violence adds another layer of political risk at a time when France is already under scrutiny over its swelling debt burden and struggle to reduce one of the euro zone's largest budget deficits. The president now finds himself trapped between bond markets demanding spending restraint and protesters demanding the opposite. Despite calls from opponents to remain in France, Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday on a Gulf tour he says will help secure fuel supplies and ease some of the economic pressures that have helped swell the ranks of the protesters. The trip carries risks, reinforcing perceptions of a president disconnected from the public mood. Images of Macron attending a Céline Dion concert with his wife Brigitte on Friday evening, hours before the unrest erupted, prompted ridicule on social media and became an easy symbol for critics seeking to portray him as detached from events. In a sign of the depth of disenchantment in parts of his political camp, some former allies have begun openly discussing whether he should leave office before the end of his term. Moreau, who spoke to Macron on Sunday, said he urged him to prepare an orderly early departure to break the current political deadlock and avoid another six months of drift. "He doesn't want to give up, that's not his character. But that's what he should do for the country," he said.

item.title: Governments warn citizens over security in France after riots
item.description: Governments in Europe and Asia, including China, on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a deterioration in security conditions after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Governments in Europe and Asia, including China, on Monday advised citizens travelling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution, warning of a [USN:L6N4650BY TEXT:"deterioration in security conditions"] after thousands were arrested and shops looted in protests over the weekend. Demonstrations across France over high prices and declining public services [USN:L1N46401W TEXT:"erupted into riots"] on Saturday, with a town hall torched as violent groups clashed with police. In response, the foreign ministries of several European countries issued fresh travel warnings. ITALY Italy said its citizens should register their presence in France on a website or an app to enable them to be located, as it warned them to avoid large crowds and exercise extreme caution. GERMANY The German foreign ministry said further riots in the coming days couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines or claims for damages if they failed to leave unauthorised demonstrations when asked to do so. CZECH REPUBLIC Czechs in France are advised to avoid demonstrations, marches and public gatherings, CTK news agency reported. The security situation in France has deteriorated, according to the Czech foreign affairs ministry. POLAND Poland said in its country guidance that visitors should avoid places where demonstrations are taking place, though there was no change to its overall guidance about whether France was safe to visit. NETHERLANDS The Dutch government in an advisory last updated on October 7 warned travelers to France to avoid protests. NORDICS Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Norway have issued advisories urging their citizens in France to avoid demonstrations and follow the guidance of local authorities. CHINA China's Foreign Ministry and diplomatic missions in France have urged Chinese nationals planning to travel to the country to remain alert to potential risks, strengthen safety precautions, and avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place, according to state media. MALAYSIA Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it is monitoring the demonstrations and that while travel to France remains unrestricted, Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves. It said its embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging Malaysians in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.

item.title: Polish satellite maker Creotech plans tenfold capacity boost, warns of Europe’s US rocket reliance
item.description: Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to raise its production capacity by up to tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said on Friday, while warning Europe would remain reliant on US rockets to put its satellites into orbit for years.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Gardawski, Marta Maciag
item.content:encoded: Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments (CRI1.WA) plans to raise its production capacity by up to tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said on Friday, while warning Europe would remain reliant on US rockets to put its satellites into orbit for years. Brona spoke with Reuters in Sopot two days after Ukraine said SpaceX (SPCX.O) had [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"curbed its use of Starshield"], the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network. Shares of Eutelsat (ETL.PA) , widely seen as Europe's leading challenger to Starlink, [USN:L8N4620IW TEXT:"jumped 23%"] on Wednesday and closed the week 28% higher. Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them. "Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of (US President) Donald Trump's administration," he said. Europe carried out 8 of the world's 324 orbital launches last year, against 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounted for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data. Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules, under which Washington can block sales of a satellite containing even a small American part. Yet it still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland's MikroGlob military programme into orbit. "Of course, Europe is waking up," Brona said, pointing to new European rocket programmes including a [USN:L1N44Y01P TEXT:"German launcher"], but added that building enough rockets would probably take a decade. Separately, he said [USN:L8N3YS0MG TEXT:"programmes"] for several large EU satellite constellations — fleets of spacecraft working as one system — were already under way, and that Creotech aimed to bid in their tenders. The satellite maker plans to open a factory in 2029 able to make 40 satellites a year of mixed types, or up to 100 of one model, compared with about 10 at its current plant. Brona added Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500-kg satellites by 2032. Revenue for next year is secured, and the company will probably sign several more contracts within six months, Brona said.
